title: FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop: All Departing Flights Grounded, Including Laredo
excerpt: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, Nov. 13, holding all departing flights across the United States — including departures from Laredo International Airport — until further notice.
content:
The Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday afternoon, Nov. 13, holding all departing flights across the United States on the ground until further notice — including departures from Laredo International Airport.

The order, issued by the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center, took effect at 2:54 p.m. Central Time. In its advisory, the FAA said all airports were ground stopped "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety."

An FAA spokesperson said a communications problem is affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle flights traveling across the country. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the ground stop followed a communication issue impacting all air traffic control centers, and that FAA technicians are investigating.

Flights already in the air are not being ordered to land immediately and will continue to their destinations. Inbound international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis, according to the advisory.

The advisory lists an effective period running through 11:30 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, but the FAA said departing traffic should remain grounded until further notice and has not given an estimate for when normal operations will return.

The last nationwide ground stop came in January 2023, when a pilot notification system failed. Before that, the last one was after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

Travelers flying out of Laredo International Airport should check their flight status with their airline before heading to the airport, as delays are expected nationwide. This is a developing story.

Update — November 13, 2026

The FAA lifted the nationwide ground stop at 8:15 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday, Nov. 13 — 7:15 p.m. Central — after more than four hours, and departures were allowed to resume, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. Recovery will be gradual, Duffy said, because it depends on whether pilots and flight attendants are available; some aircraft will not move until Saturday morning. FlightAware counted nearly 5,000 flights canceled on Friday, with nearly 800 cancellations already listed for Saturday, and aviation analytics firm Cirium counted 827 diverted flights as of 7:05 p.m. Eastern, according to the Associated Press.

Duffy said at a White House briefing that radar and communications data became unstable at en route centers and terminal radar facilities, and that overloaded older switches and routers were producing inconsistent data. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said investigators have found no indication of a cyberattack so far, but have not ruled one out. The investigation into the cause continues.

Update — November 16, 2026

The FAA said on Sunday, Nov. 15, that investigators had traced the communications failure to two sites: a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, where the agency's network provider, L3Harris, had been doing work that included installing a new router. The agency said its aging telecommunications network received about 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overloading switches and routers, and that the disruption affected 17 of the FAA's 22 en route control centers. The FAA ruled out a cyberattack, saying there was no indication of an external malicious actor, and said its SMART airspace-management platform, which expanded nationwide on Nov. 10, did not cause the outage. The FAA counted about 12,462 flights canceled on Nov. 13, though it said not all were directly caused by the ground stop, and said about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landed safely. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said air travel was back at full operations on Saturday morning and that he expects systems to return to normal before Thanksgiving travel.

Update — November 20, 2026

Investigators have now reproduced the router failure that triggered the November 13 ground stop, but they still do not know why it happened. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said November 17 that the failure at the El Dorado, Arkansas, site was recreated in testing at contractor L3Harris's laboratory in Florida. "We've been able to recreate what happened in El Dorado, but the root cause of what happened, we don't have clarity yet," Duffy said. The Federal Aviation Administration has paused further installations of the Juniper routers at the center of the investigation while testing continues, the agency confirmed. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Thursday that investigators are "very close" to determining the root cause and that Duffy plans to brief the public on the findings. Reuters reported the three-day disruption from November 13 to 16 canceled more than 18,000 flights and delayed nearly 28,000, affecting more than 1 million passengers. Duffy has also asked Congress for another $50 billion to modernize air traffic control, on top of $12.5 billion approved last year.

Source: Federal Aviation Administration advisory, Nov. 13, 2026, as reported by USA Today, CNN and Reuters. Update sources: Associated Press, as reported by Airways Magazine and Watchers News, Nov. 13, 2026; FAA Command Center notice. Nov. 16 update sources: Federal Aviation Administration, Nov. 15, 2026, as reported by The Cincinnati Enquirer, Travel Weekly and TechRepublic. Nov. 20 update sources: Reuters, November 19, 2026; CNN, November 19, 2026; Investor's Business Daily, November 20, 2026; Travel Market News, November 20, 2026; TravelHost, November 20, 2026.
